table.brief: A/B test results: Metric / Control (mean, 95% CI) / Variant (mean, 95% CI) / Lift / p-value

understanding.purpose: Compare checkout outcomes between control and variant, including effect size and statistical evidence across seven metrics.
understanding.reading: Readers scan metric names down the first column, compare each control mean with its variant mean and confidence intervals, then check lift and p-value. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.
groups: Control mean and 95% CI belong together, as do variant mean and 95% CI; corresponding control and variant columns should have comparable widths.
Lift and p-value summarize the difference and its statistical evidence, so they form a related pair.
keep_intact: Numeric values, percentages, currency amounts, time values, confidence interval endpoints and p-values should remain intact where possible.
Metric names should remain recognizable, with individual words kept intact where space permits.
may_wrap: Metric names can wrap at spaces; longer names can use additional row height.
Confidence intervals may wrap at a range separator if necessary, while keeping each endpoint intact.
Grouped headers can wrap if needed.

preferred.name: r1B
preferred.note: Give metric names more room to improve their rhythm and reduce row height, while keeping the paired numeric columns consistent and allowing intervals to wrap.

acceptable.name: r1C
acceptable.note: Explore a wider, easier-to-scan table with more generous labels and complete intervals on one line. This costs additional horizontal scrolling but keeps each row's values together.

acceptable.name: r3A
acceptable.note: Widen the metric column enough to improve label rhythm while retaining the more economical interval widths. Give both mean columns 73px so their longest values fit on one line.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Combine r2B's readable metric labels with r2C's single-line confidence intervals. This accepts more scrolling for a compact table with intact values.

bad.name: r2A
bad.note: Keep corresponding mean and interval columns nearly equal while narrowing the metric column enough to show both means within the initial viewport. Allow longer labels and intervals to wrap without splitting words.
bad.why: The narrow metric column produces several three-line labels and a four-line label. The narrow mean columns also break the checkout times across lines, making rows harder to scan.

bad.name: r2B
bad.note: Give metric names more room while narrowing both interval columns equally. This tests whether shorter labels and less horizontal scrolling outweigh additional interval wrapping.
bad.why: The narrow confidence-interval columns fragment several ranges, including the checkout-time interval across three lines; the mean times also wrap. This disrupts numerical comparisons.

bad.name: r2C
bad.note: Keep complete confidence intervals on one line, but narrow the metric and mean columns to reduce scrolling compared with r1C. This tests a clearer interval-first layout with a more compact initial view.
bad.why: Long metric labels wrap to three or four lines and mean times wrap, despite the substantial horizontal scrolling required by the wide confidence-interval columns.

bad.name: r3C
bad.note: Fit the metric, control mean and interval, and variant mean within 359px so the first comparison is visible on arrival. Allow metric labels and intervals to wrap, while giving both intervals equal width.
bad.why: The narrow metric column creates several tall rows, including a four-line label, while the first viewport still cuts through the variant group.

rationale: r1B gives metric names enough space to remain recognizable while keeping mean values intact and corresponding control and variant columns balanced. Confidence intervals wrap, but their columns are substantially narrower than in r3B, reducing the distance needed to reach lift and p-value. The first viewport shows the metric and control columns plus the beginning of the variant group, inviting comparison across the scroll.

general: Give row identifiers enough width to preserve recognizable phrases and a steady scanning rhythm.
Columns with parallel roles should have similar widths and wrapping behavior.
Judge horizontal scrolling alongside the readability gained by wider columns.
specific: Mean values need about 73px including padding to keep the checkout times on one line.
The confidence intervals need much more width to stay on one line, so wrapping them saves substantial horizontal space.
The long support-contacts label sets a practical limit on how narrow the metric column can be.

tradeoffs: r3B keeps the intervals on one line and produces shorter rows, but requires substantially more scrolling and shows none of the variant values in the initial viewport. r3A saves a little width at the cost of an additional tall row.
uncertain: A designer prioritizing intact confidence intervals over initial visibility and scroll distance could reasonably prefer r3B. The ranges are conservative estimates around r1B, not browser-verified thresholds; changing several columns together may alter wrapping or the viewport boundary.

critique.good: The metric names are recognizable, the numerical values and intervals stay on one line, and the paired control and variant columns have consistent proportions. Rows remain easy to follow.
critique.problems: Only the control group and a sliver of the variant group appear in the initial viewport. The wide intervals create substantial horizontal travel before readers can compare the variant, lift, and p-value.
critique.cause: The 134px and 131px confidence interval columns preserve entire ranges on one line, but they account for much of the 691px table width.

critique.good: The narrower interval columns bring the variant mean into the initial viewport and reduce scrolling. Most ranges wrap into readable endpoints, and corresponding groups remain similarly sized.
critique.problems: The word 'abandonment' splits across lines, weakening the row label. The support-contact label takes four lines, and the time means wrap even though they are short values.
critique.cause: The 120px metric column leaves 99px for text, just under the 100px longest word. The 71px and 70px mean columns leave too little room for the complete time values; the 90px interval columns deliberately trade single-line ranges for less scrolling.

critique.good: All seven columns are visible at once, so the group structure and the existence of lift and p-value can be seen without scrolling.
critique.problems: Headers, metric names, numbers, and p-values fragment across lines. Rows become very tall, and readers must reconstruct values before they can compare them.
critique.cause: Widths of 39–49px leave only 18–28px for most numeric cells, while the 100px metric column leaves 79px for labels. These widths are far below the space needed to keep the content intact.

critique.good: The initial viewport shows metric names, the complete control group and the variant mean. Corresponding columns have equal widths, and values avoid mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Metric labels occupy up to four lines, making rows tall and the table harder to scan. Several confidence intervals wrap, while the remaining variant and summary columns require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 121px metric column leaves only 100px for text; the 90px confidence-interval columns leave 69px, insufficient for longer ranges.

critique.good: The wider metric column reduces the tallest labels to three lines and gives the table a calmer vertical rhythm. Numeric values remain intact, and corresponding groups retain balanced widths.
critique.problems: Some labels and confidence intervals still take multiple lines. The viewport cuts through the variant mean, so the reader must scroll even to compare both means.
critique.cause: The 150px metric column improves wrapping but pushes the variant mean beyond the 360px viewport; 90px confidence-interval columns still wrap longer ranges.

critique.good: Confidence intervals fit on one line, making their endpoints easy to compare. The metric column keeps labels reasonably compact, and the control and variant groups have comparable proportions.
critique.problems: The wider intervals do not reduce the table height relative to r1B, because metric labels determine the tallest rows. The first viewport ends at the control group, and the large overall width makes comparisons more scroll-intensive.
critique.cause: The 134px and 131px confidence-interval columns accommodate full ranges but add 85px to the table width compared with r1B.

critique.good: The control and variant columns have balanced widths, and the initial viewport shows the metric, control results, and variant mean. Words and numeric endpoints remain intact.
critique.problems: Metric labels create tall, uneven rows, particularly the four-line support-contacts label. Confidence intervals also wrap, and the time mean occupies two lines. The variant interval, lift, and p-value require scrolling.
critique.cause: The 123px metric column leaves 102px for text; the 88px interval columns leave 67px, and the mean columns leave about 50px.

critique.good: The wider metric column makes the labels easier to scan and produces a compact, regular table. Corresponding control and variant columns remain balanced, with no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: The narrower confidence intervals wrap frequently; the control time interval takes three lines. The viewport cuts through the variant mean, making the first comparison less immediately readable. Lift and p-value remain offscreen.
critique.cause: The 165px metric column consumes 42px more than in r2A, while the 79px interval columns leave only 58px for text.

critique.good: Both confidence interval columns accommodate their longest values on one line, making intervals easy to read and compare after scrolling. Corresponding columns have similar widths.
critique.problems: The narrow metric column still creates tall, uneven rows, so the extra interval width does not reduce the table height. The viewport cuts into the variant mean, and the wide table demands the most scrolling.
critique.cause: The 123px metric column remains the height constraint, while the 134px and 131px interval columns add 89px in total compared with r2A.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r2A.why: Metric labels remain readable, and the control group and variant mean mostly fit initially. Several confidence intervals and time values wrap, making comparisons slower.

r1B.why: The metric column gives most labels comfortable line breaks, and means stay intact. Confidence intervals wrap, and the viewport cuts through the variant mean column.

r3A.why: Metric labels and means are generally readable, with a useful initial view of control and variant means. Confidence intervals wrap, and the variant column is cut at the viewport edge.

ref_equal.why: Everything fits within the viewport, but headers, metric names, numbers and p-values split across fragments. The resulting tall rows are very difficult to scan.

ref_auto.why: The initial view reaches the variant confidence interval, but narrow columns wrap several labels, time values and intervals into multiple lines, weakening row-by-row comparison.

r1C.why: Metric labels, means and control confidence intervals remain intact or wrap naturally. The initial view shows the complete control group, though comparing it with the variant requires horizontal scrolling.

raw.unsure: The supplied views do not show the full right-hand portions of the scrolling layouts, so the widths and wrapping of variant, lift and p-value columns cannot be assessed completely. The trade-off between F's intact intervals and the earlier glimpse of variant means in B and C is also close.

r1C.why: Metric labels and control values remain readable, with confidence intervals intact, but the viewport ends before the variant results, making comparison dependent on scrolling.

r2A.why: Both means fit at first sight, supporting comparison. Some metric labels and confidence intervals wrap heavily, and the variant interval and later results require scrolling.

ref_equal.why: Everything fits the viewport, but words, numbers, headers and p-values break across lines, making the table very difficult to read.

r3A.why: Metric labels have room and most values read clearly. The variant mean sits at the viewport edge, however, and several confidence intervals wrap.

r1B.why: The metric labels are readable and the control mean stays intact, but the variant mean is cut by the viewport edge and confidence intervals wrap.

ref_auto.why: Both means appear in the viewport, but narrow metric and interval columns cause frequent wrapping, including awkward breaks in the time values.

raw.unsure: The supplied views show only the left portion of the scrolling layouts, so I cannot assess the widths and readability of all off-screen columns.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
